title: Jerusalem rebuilt
hookLine: blessings for Jerusalem and for the line of David

lines: A GLASS UNDER THE GROOM'S FOOT.
cards: At the end of a Jewish wedding, just before the cheering, the groom stamps on a glass wrapped in cloth. It shatters, and everyone shouts mazel tov.
Many explain the broken glass as a memory of Jerusalem's destroyed Temple, brought into the middle of the celebration. Even here, the city is remembered.
Three times a day, in the middle of the Amidah, there's a prayer that does the opposite of breaking. It asks for the city to be built.

teach.b: The fourteenth blessing says: to Jerusalem, Your city, return in mercy, and dwell in it as You promised. Rebuild it soon, in our days, as an everlasting building, and quickly set up the throne of David within it.
Blessed are You, who builds Jerusalem. Notice the tense. Not who will build, or who built.
Who builds: an ongoing act, a work site that never closes.

The fifteenth blessing goes on to the family of David: may the branch of David Your servant sprout soon, for we hope for Your salvation all day long. Blessed are You, who makes the horn of salvation sprout.
Branch, sprout: the Hebrew is tzemach, a prophets' image for a king from David's line, whom Jewish tradition calls mashiach, the anointed one, the messiah.
Reform Judaism has generally spoken instead of a messianic age, a repaired world, rather than one person; Orthodox Judaism keeps the hope of a king from David's line.
Some early prayer texts found in the Cairo Geniza show that in the land of Israel these two were once a single blessing.

teach.h: PRAY FOR THE PEACE OF JERUSALEM.
teach.b: The Psalms put it simply, in the old Jewish translation: "Pray for the peace of Jerusalem." On the afternoon of the fast of Tisha b'Av, the day of mourning for the Temples, a paragraph of comfort is added right here.
But on ordinary days the blessing isn't a lament. It's construction language.
Rebuild. Sprout. Every day, a little more.

how: The weekday Amidah's fourteenth blessing prays for the rebuilding of Jerusalem and the fifteenth for the branch of David; on the afternoon of Tisha b'Av the paragraph Nachem, a prayer of comfort, is added to the Jerusalem blessing.

games.q: you're writing the ending of a blessing about Jerusalem. which tense do the rabbis choose?
o: who will one day build Jerusalem.
games.why: boneh Yerushalayim: who builds. the building is treated as going on now, every day.

practice: Choose one thing in your life that's broken and could, slowly, be rebuilt: a relationship, a neighborhood, your health after a hard year, your trust in yourself.

Don't plan the whole thing; picture one brick, the first small piece that could go back in place, and hold the hope that it can be built, in its time. If you pray, you can join that hope to the prayer for Jerusalem.
